item.description: The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) has blessed seven C++ language revisions since 1998. The language is mostly developed by ISO's Working Group 21, which considers proposed additions and amendments, integrates them into a document, and then presents that document to the main ISO body to be voted on as a standard. On October 23, for the first time ever, ISO declined to ratify a document presented by Working Group 21, leaving the future of the C++26 standard in doubt. The decision was driven by controversy around a proposed new "contracts" feature that would add pre- and post-conditions to function signatures.
item.title: [$] C++26 contract confusion

item.description: Buildroot maintainer Peter Korsgaard gave a presentation about the long history of the build tool for embedded Linux systems at the 2026 Embedded Linux Conference Europe. In it, he covered more than just the past 25 years, looking at the current status of the project as well as what to expect in Buildroot's future. It was an interesting view inside this long-running project that has been a mainstay of the embedded-Linux world throughout almost all of this century.
item.title: [$] 25 years of Buildroot

item.description: Futexes are a kernel subsystem that provides support for fast mutexes in user space. While futexes can indeed be fast, they are not fast enough for a number of users. Partly as a result of that, the implementation of futexes has grown in complexity over the years, with two basic variants on offer. The desire for faster futexes remains, though, and that inspires new patches, including this series from Suleiman Souhlal adding a third futex class called "futex PING" for "priority inheritance next generation".
item.title: [$] A new generation of futexes

item.description: Zellij is a relatively new entrant in the terminal-multiplexer category. Like GNU Screen and tmux it gives users the ability to manage a workspace inside a terminal with split panes, provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, version 0.46, adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings screen so users can configure the application without fussing with configuration files. While the low version number might suggest that it is not yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to meet the needs of many users.
item.title: [$] Zellij manages terminal workspaces with style

item.description: Version 1.13 of Julia was released on September 10, 2026. Julia is a general-purpose language especially well suited to high-performance numerical computing. Its expressiveness, speed, and composability have made it increasingly popular with scientists and mathematicians. We last looked at Julia one year ago, in a review of the 1.12 release. The newest version features an enhanced read-eval-print loop (REPL), a GUI for installation, a smoother developer experience, and an assortment of performance improvements.
item.title: [$] Julia 1.13 brings REPL improvements and more

item.description: The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.
item.title: [$] Added indirection allows for larger BPF programs

item.description: The openSUSE Project has been working on the Agama installer for four years; it was the default installer for openSUSE Leap 16.0 when it was released in 2025, and has been adopted by other openSUSE flavors as well. Now the project is gearing up to go all-in on Agama for Tumbleweed, the rolling-release edition that is meant to be where updates and new features land first. Even so, the community has concerns about losing some of YaST's legacy functionality and the impact on installing Tumbleweed on systems that have less RAM.
item.title: [$] Bringing the Agama installer to openSUSE Tumbleweed

item.description: The 7.4-rc4 kernel is out for testing. Linus said: "It's huge. What a surprise. Lots of little fixes all over, with drivers being pretty exactly half of it (gpu and networking showing up as usual, but there's usb, iio, nvme, sound.. you name it)."
item.title: Kernel prepatch 7.4-rc4

item.description: CachyOS, a performance-focused distribution based on Arch Linux, has announced its November 2026 release. Notable changes in this release include a new recovery environment ("cachyos-recovery") for rolling back broken systems, Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) v2 support for games that require EAC to run, version 2.0.0 of the CachyOS Package Installer, and more.
item.title: CachyOS November 2026 release

item.description:
The Internet Society has announced that the Jonathan B. Postel Service Award has been awarded to Dave Täht for his many efforts to improve the Internet.

Täht's legacy can be found in community hubs in Nicaragua, where he worked to expand connectivity, and first discovered the urgency of solving bufferbloat. It can be found in every lag-free video call with a loved one. It can be found in outer space—Täht helped Starlink solve its latency challenges. And it can be found in the countless people he mentored and befriended over the years, who will not stop until bufferbloat stops getting in the way of band practice.

Dave is still deeply missed by those of us who knew him; this is an award he richly deserved.
item.title: Dave Täht given the Jonathan B. Postel Service Award

item.description: Early in the 7.4 merge window, Greg Kroah-Hartman applied a patch that caused the kernel to be marked as tainted whenever user space manually binds or unbinds a device driver to a device. This change was meant to be a defense against a flood of spurious bug reports generated by fuzzers, but it also turned out to get in the way of some real use cases. After some discussion, the patch has been reverted, but this situation hints at an area where better kernel interfaces are needed.
item.title: [$] Tainting (or not) on manual driver binding

item.description:
Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...]

Today, more than 99.5% of all lines of code ever contributed to LLVM are either covered by the new license, too small for copyright to apply, or no longer in the repository.

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.
item.title: Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort

item.description:
Version 8.3.1 of Vim Classic—a long-term support fork of Vim maintained without LLM assistance—has been released.

This release includes applicable Vim patches up to Vim 8.2.3237, including numerous bug fixes, minor features, and compatibility improvements for Vim plugins. This release also removes Python 2 support from Vim Classic.

The full list of changes in this release is available on sourcehut.
